newsitem.title: USA: Russia banker sees shakeup, 400 banks face closure.
newsitem.headline: Russia banker sees shakeup, 400 banks face closure.

text.p: The Russian banking industry is in the midst of upheaval and 400 banks could lose their licenses to operate this year, a prominent Russian banker said.
"About 35 percent of Russian banks are in trouble," said Yakov Dubenetsky, chairman of the board of Promstroybank, one of Russia's largest banks.
Surveying the banking industry in an interview with Reuters, Dubenetsky said Thursday that falling inflation has squeezed profits from the lucrative money market operations.
"A year ago, banks can make 150 percent profit. Now they make 30 to 35 percent," he said.
The upheaval in the industry drove 500 banks out of business last year, he said. Of the surviving 2,200 banks, another 400 are in the process of having their licenses revoked, he added.
But about 1,000 banks are solvent and top-tier banks may thrive in the new environment, he said.
Dubenetsky was in New York for the opening of its representative office here.
His institution is the first Russian bank to establish operations in the United States, according to the New York State Department of Banking.
Promstroybank is the sixth largest bank in Russia, he said.
Dubenetsky said Russian banks are tightening security to fight theft and improve their public image as "custodians," he said.
Dubenetsky believed the banks should bear the responsibility for security lapses to protect customers, but he emphasized such "episodes" were few and far between.
One widely-reported scandal was the theft of Finance Ministry (MinFin) bonds last year in the financial sector.
He said an employee of one bank, which he did not identify, stole MinFin bonds which belonged to Promstroybank.
On the positive side, the central bank has curbed inflation, projected at about 13 to 14 percent this year, he said.
Russian government figures show inflation for 1996 tumbled below 22 percent, from 131 percent in the previous year.
But Dubenetsky noted a gloomier picture regarding economic growth, hindered by insufficient capital.
"Russian deposits consist of short-term deposits," he said. "We don't have long-term capital"
Dubenetsky estimated that Russia needs a total of $100 billion to $300 billion in direct foreign investment. Last year, it only attracted $4 biilion to $6 billion, he added.
Russia's gross domestic product fell by six percent last year, according to government figures released Monday.
Dubenetsky said the New York representative office of the Promstroybank seeks to drum up investments and to serve as a conduit to capital-hungry Russian industries.
"We need investment sources of foreign capital, technical expertise and management skills."
Russia is racing against the clock to put its economic house in order before simmering social unrest boils to the top, he added.
"Our economy has to run effectively," he said. "We may have two to three years before social problems grow up."
Regarding President Boris Yeltsin's health, Dubenetsky said the illness might have slowed down the passing of certain reform measures.
"Yeltsin is a strong man and a fighter," Dubenetsky said. "He has surprised many people and he will get well."
